title: Two Dreams in an Egyptian Prison
overview: While unjustly held in prison, Joseph correctly explains the dreams of two royal servants, but the one who is freed forgets to help him.

parts.label: Royal servants jailed (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: The cupbearer, a trusted official who served the king his wine, and the chief baker angered Pharaoh, and the text never says how. They were held in the same prison as Joseph, and he was put in charge of looking after them.

parts.label: A troubling night (vv. 5-8)
parts.note: In Egypt, dreams were read by trained experts, so the two men were upset to have no one in prison who could explain theirs. Joseph notices their sadness and says the true meaning comes from God, not from any expert's skill.

parts.label: The cupbearer's dream (vv. 9-15)
parts.note: The vine, grapes and cup picture the man back at his old job, and Joseph says that within three days Pharaoh will "lift up his head," meaning call him back to honor. Joseph then asks to be remembered, saying only that he was taken from his homeland and is innocent here, without naming those who wronged him.

parts.label: The baker's dream (vv. 16-19)
parts.note: Servants really did carry stacked baskets of food on their heads, and birds stealing from them was a familiar sight. Joseph turns the same phrase grimly: Pharaoh will lift off the baker's head, and his body will be left on a pole for birds, which meant being denied a proper burial.

parts.label: Fulfilled, then forgotten (vv. 20-23)
parts.note: At Pharaoh's birthday feast, both cases are decided exactly as Joseph said: one man restored, the other executed. The chapter ends bluntly, with the freed cupbearer forgetting Joseph entirely, leaving him still in prison.

think: Joseph helps someone who then forgets him; what do you think it takes to keep being kind when kindness goes unreturned?
